I have been farming this 8 mu of land in Quzhou for 25 years. My father taught me how to work this soil, and I have watched it every season since. My household has six mouths, but two of my children work in the city and send money home, so I can afford good inputs — though I am not one to waste money on things the land does not need. We have a well, so water is there when the crops call for it.

For wheat, I will plant an improved variety from the seed station, the same kind my neighbors grow. After the maize comes off in autumn, I run the rotary tiller to break up the soil and bury the stubble. I spread compound fertilizer as a basal dressing and then topdress with urea at green-up and again at jointing — wheat is hungry, especially in spring. I irrigate four times: winter irrigation to protect the seedlings from the cold, then at green-up, jointing, and grain filling. I spray three times: herbicide once to keep the weeds down, and insecticide mixed with fungicide twice when the aphids and rust show up. If the weather holds, I expect about 1,000 jin per mu.

For maize, I buy hybrid seed every year — Nongda or Denghai, whatever the shop has that year. After we harvest the wheat in June, there is no time to lose, so I sow directly into the wheat stubble without tilling. The stubble keeps the soil moist. I put compound fertilizer down with the seed and side-dress a little urea when the plants reach the big-trumpet stage. Maize does not drink as much as wheat; two irrigations are enough, one at silking and one at grain filling. I spray herbicide before emergence and insecticide once for corn borers. I expect around 1,100 jin per mu.

This is how I have always done it, and it puts food on the table.
